A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhysChoreo, with readable text, equations, tables and figures that can be matched reliably. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; both refer to separate supplementary material that is outside the supplied evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original physical-property prediction experiments, generated-video evaluations, a 31-person preference study and component/loss ablations in Tables 1–5.

after.justification: v2 retains original prediction, video-evaluation and ablation results, and reports additional PhysCtrl comparisons and qualitative part-level and failure analyses.

M1.justification: The predictor architecture, four loss components, editable physics simulation and video-generation pipeline are retained. v2 specifies discretization and transition constraints previously described more generally; these disclosures do not establish a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: v2 Figure 7 adds qualitative hammer-impact and wind-driven flower scenarios for examining part-specific dynamics. The principal prediction/video tasks and the 9,580-sample, 24-category PartNet-derived dataset, including its counterfactual examples, remain unchanged.

E2.justification: PhysCtrl, previously discussed only as related work, joins the reported video comparisons in v2 Tables 2–3 and Figure 5. Figure 7 also replaces the direct-generation/trajectory-conditioning comparisons with manually specified global-physics controls. The three physical-property baselines remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported video preference comparison expands from five to six methods. The replacement qualitative ablation compares manual global physics with part-level prediction using the same simulator and video pipeline. The principal sample counts and metrics remain unchanged; newly specified material-mapping details do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1's video-conditioning ablation compares direct generation, noisy trajectory initialization and trajectory control. v2 replaces it with a global-versus-part-level physics comparison and adds a rendering failure case in Section 5.5/Figure 7. The quantitative architecture and loss ablations in Tables 4–5 are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The revised scores and preference percentages do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds PhysCtrl VLM scores of 3.75/4.25/4.30 for SA/PC/VQ and revises user preferences: PhysChoreo's Total changes from 58.48% to 50.1% with the expanded comparator set, not a comparable-setting decline. Tables 1, 4 and 5 and existing methods' VLM scores remain unchanged. Figure 7 replaces conditioning findings with part-response and rendering-failure results.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds a formal within-part neighborhood graph and weighted discrete approximation of wave-speed smoothness. Section 3.3 adds temporal-smoothing and shared stiffness-rescaling equations, including the relative-stiffness preservation property. These are limited mathematical specifications; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about the dataset, part-aware physics prediction, temporally editable simulation and controllable video generation. Additional comparisons do not change the scope of those claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of global versus part-specific dynamics and identifies lighting/shadow artifacts from the video-rendering stage despite stable simulated trajectories. It removes the earlier interpretation of alternative conditioning strategies. Limitations concerning large scenes and internal physical states remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies training on two A6000 GPUs, discrete loss computation, temporal smoothing and stiffness bounds. It also documents six-category prompting for the VLM baselines, Pixie's permissive mapping for plastic, and that ablation iterations denote early-stopping epochs. These are disclosures rather than established changes to existing runs; the project link is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to the GPT-5 system card and S2AM3D. Other reference changes largely update publication metadata or numbering, while the related-work discussion and positioning remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 expands explanations and definitions in Sections 3.2–3.3, revises the final ablation subsection, and adds a failure-case subsection, keywords and acknowledgements. Most narrative text and the main section order are retained, with limited copyediting.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from a two-column layout to a narrower single-column format, relocating and resizing figures and tables. Figure 4 is rearranged, Figure 6 becomes a two-by-two display, Figure 5 gains a PhysCtrl row, and Figure 7 is replaced. The user-study and VLM tables swap numbering and appear side by side.

improvement.justification: v2 improves technical auditability through explicit loss/simulator specifications, clearer baseline handling, an evaluated PhysCtrl comparison and a concrete failure case. These gains are limited by removal of the conditioning ablation and a new reporting inconsistency: the user-study Total percentages sum to 101.32%, versus 100% in v1. Overall, the documentation and evaluation improve modestly without establishing better model performance.
